name: Chêne de Nerthe

location.address: In the pine forest near the hamlet of Nerthe, on an old airial (forest clearing with house ruins), commune of Magescq

access: Free, on foot. The tree stands on privately owned pine-plantation land within an old airial but is openly and regularly visited by hikers, joggers and mountain bikers via a forestry track from the Nerthe hamlet (about 1km walk each way, difficult by car); no gate, fence or restriction signage was found in any source. The Magescq tourist office also runs a separate, optional guided minibus tour in summer (booking required for that specific tour only, not for general access).
transport: No public transport reaches the site. Nearest town with an SNCF station is Dax (TGV), roughly 10km away; from there it is a drive to the forestry track near Nerthe hamlet, then a ~1km walk on foot.
verify_notes: Officially labelled 'Arbre Remarquable de France' by the A.R.B.R.E.S. association on 18 September 2010 (mairie-magescq.fr, the commune's own site). Girth 6.50m at 1.30m height per the official label and the commune (one source gives 6.40m at 1.60m, a plausible measurement-height difference, not a contradiction worth flagging hard). Height 27m. Age: locally believed 600 years; independently, circumference/diameter growth-rate estimation methods cited in the krapooarboricole blog give 500-600 years; the official label rounds this to '600 to 700 years'. Used the wider band (500-700) to stay honest about the spread. GPS coordinates logged by an independent tree enthusiast in 2009 (N43-7651988 / W001-1172886) match our candidate coordinates to 4-5 decimal places, so the pin is tree-level, not just park-level. Species: search results consistently title the monumentaltrees.com page 'Chene pedoncule' (Pedunculate Oak / Quercus robur), which matches the common oak of Landes airials, but monumentaltrees.com 403s automated fetches (documented site behaviour) so I could not open the page directly to confirm; flagging curation_status for this reason rather than for the tree's identity or existence, which are solid. History: in an old 'airial' (a Landes forest clearing with ruined farm buildings), isolated 2-3km from the nearest house, known mainly to hikers/joggers/mountain bikers before its 2010 label. A major branch (3.3m circumference) fell in August 2010; comments through 2011-2012 discuss tar treatment of the wound and continued visits, so the tree was alive and visited well after the branch loss. Continued relevance: regional tourist board (tourismelandes.com) lists it as a natural-heritage point, and hiking-route sites (AllTrails, Cirkwi, Sitytrail, decathlon-outdoor) show routes built to it as recently as February 2023, which is the best 'still alive and still visited' evidence available short of a dated photo. Destination test: this is a niche regional attraction, not a national one, but it carries a genuine official designation (not just a register listing), dedicated hiking routes across four different platforms, an organised tourist-office tour, and at least one online account (2012) of someone visiting the Landes specifically hunting for this tree without finding it the first time. On balance I would say it clears the single-tree-destination bar for a determined tree-visitor, but it is a close call; whoever writes it up should keep the framing modest (a rewarding forest walk to a genuinely remarkable oak) rather than overselling it as a headline attraction.

name: If commun de Nicorps

location.address: Churchyard of the Eglise Saint-Corneille, Nicorps

access: Free. It stands in the churchyard/cemetery of the Eglise Saint-Corneille, a village church with a public cemetery, open in daylight hours; no restriction found in any source.
transport: No specific transit stop found. Nicorps is a small village about 6km south-west of Coutances (which has an SNCF station); reaching the village itself requires a car or bicycle from Coutances.
verify_notes: Female common yew (Taxus baccata) in the churchyard of Eglise Saint-Corneille, Nicorps. Wikimanche's article on the church states it is aged 600 years and classified 'Arbre remarquable de France' (the same national A.R.B.R.E.S. label as candidate #1 in this batch, the Chene de Nerthe). Separately, Wikimanche's departmental list of remarkable trees records 'If de Nicorps' as labelled by the CAUE de la Manche (the regional architecture/planning/environment council) in January 2009, likely the same designation event referred to from a different angle, though I could not fully confirm the two labels are one and the same rather than sequential regional-then-national recognitions. Measurement history, from the Coutances Tourisme / CAUE dossier: naturalist and photographer Henri Gadeau de Kerville measured it on 11 June 1930 at 6.28m girth and 18.50m height, as part of his survey 'Les vieux arbres de la Normandie'. On 10 November 1998 CAUE de la Manche recorded storm damage from the October 1987 hurricane: the tree had lost a major limb, height had dropped to under 12m, but girth had grown to 7.15m. The same dossier compares aerial photos from 25 July 1947 to a later date showing canopy regression on the north-east side, but notes the tree had since regrown to 16m, which it gives as evidence of continued vitality. I used the 1998 girth (715cm) as the recorded figure since it is the latest measured one on file; note the source itself calls it 'circonference croissante' (still growing) so it is likely larger today. IMPORTANT DISAGREEMENT: a 2013 Wikimedia Commons photo of this tree is captioned by its photographer 'L'if millenaire' (the millennial yew), i.e. roughly 1000 years old, which is well above the 600 years given by the church's own Wikimanche article; I have not found a source for the 1000-year claim beyond that one caption, so I am treating it as an uncorroborated popular claim and using the official 600-year figure as primary, with a wide band (500-700) to stay honest. Notable burials in the same churchyard per Wikimanche: missionary Pere Louis Joseph Calenge, professor Stephen Chauvet, and Emile Daireaux (founder of the town of Daireaux, Argentina). Location precision: the CAUE dossier and Gadeau de Kerville's account both imply the churchyard holds TWO yews ('l'autre if du cimetiere, plus gros', i.e. this document is about 'the OTHER yew of the cemetery, the bigger one'), so there are at least two candidate trunks in a small space; I cannot be certain the given coordinate pins the specific bigger/documented one rather than its smaller neighbour, though both would stand within a few metres of each other in the same small enclosed churchyard, so any error is minor. Marking location_precision approximate and curation_status flagged for that reason. Alive evidence: best dated evidence is the July 2013 Commons photograph (over a decade old, not 'the last few years'); I found nothing more recent in the time available, so this should be treated as thinner alive-evidence than ideal, though nothing suggests the tree has died or been felled either. Destination test: this is a well-documented, twice-officially-labelled ancient yew with real written history back to 1930, but it is a modest village churchyard tree rather than a headline attraction; I doubt it clears the bar as a dedicated single-tree destination on its own, more a worthwhile stop for someone already touring the Coutances/Cotentin area or visiting other Manche yews (several other old yews are cited in the same region: La Lucerne-d'Outremer, Le Chefresne, Saint-Ursin). Recommend weighing this carefully before giving it a standalone page.

name: If de Jauzé

location.address: Le bourg, next to the church, 72110 Jauzé

access: Free (confirmed explicitly by the regional tourism board's own listing: 'Acces au site gratuit: Oui'). It stands in the village ('le bourg'), by the church, not on enclosed private land.
transport: No public transport found serving Jauzé, a small village in Sarthe; reachable by car. Nearest larger town is La Ferte-Bernard (SEPENES, the association that inventories Sarthe's remarkable trees, is based there), a short drive away.
verify_notes: Male-flowering common yew (Taxus baccata), described by SEPENES (the Sarthe environmental association that runs the department's own inventory of remarkable trees) as 'le doyen de la Sarthe' (the oldest tree in the department), 'quelque 7 a 9 siecles' (roughly 700 to 900 years) and 5.70m in circumference. It is also officially labelled 'arbre remarquable' and, per the Pays de la Loire regional tourism board's own page, is 'the only male-flowering yew classified in Sarthe', a genuine distinguishing fact worth using. Local legend (explicitly flagged as legend by the tourism board, not fact) says it was planted by Vikings 800 to 1000 years ago; a Dutch caption on the Commons photo separately calls it the 'Duizendjarige' (thousand-year-old) yew, an unsourced popular claim in the same direction. I used SEPENES's more conservative, source-attributed '7 to 9 centuries' as the primary estimate rather than the millennium claims, and noted the legend for the writer rather than folding it into the numbers. Location: the Commons photo (25 August 2012, photographer Pymouss, a prolific OSM/Commons contributor) is tagged to an OpenStreetMap node (10102580506) with a camera location of 48.212222, 0.378056, which matches our given coordinate essentially exactly, so this is a tree-level pin (an individually mapped OSM node), not a village-level guess. Category 'If de Jauze' exists as its own Commons category. Access: the regional tourism board's own practical-info field states free access explicitly ('Acces au site gratuit: Oui'), and it stands in the open village centre next to the church rather than on enclosed grounds. Alive evidence: best dated evidence found is the August 2012 photograph; I could not find anything more recent within the time budget (the Sarthe Tourisme page for it, sarthetourisme.com, blocked automated fetches behind a Cloudflare challenge, and the Office de Tourisme Maine Saosnois page found in search results now 404s, suggesting it may have been reorganised rather than that the tree is gone). Both the SEPENES and Pays de la Loire regional tourism pages are live, current pages as of this pass, which is circumstantial but not dated evidence of continued existence. Destination test: this is the most credentialed of the three yews I looked at in this batch (an explicit, sourced 'oldest tree in the department' claim, an official remarkable-tree label, a genuinely rare biological fact in its male-flowering status, and coverage from both a departmental environmental association and the regional tourism board), but it is still a small-village churchyard-adjacent tree rather than a nationally famous one. I would lean towards this one clearing the single-tree-destination bar for someone specifically collecting France's oldest yews, more so than the Nicorps yew in this same batch, but it is a regional rather than national draw.

name: Le Sully de Pesselières

location.address: Pesselières, a hamlet of the commune of Sougères-en-Puisaye

access: Free. It stands in the open hamlet of Pesselières (references place it near the 'rue du chateau' and 'place des halles', both public streets/square), not on enclosed private land.
transport: No public transport found. Pesselières is a small hamlet within Sougères-en-Puisaye, Yonne (Burgundy); reachable by car or as part of a countryside walk (Visorando lists 13 different hiking routes passing it).
verify_notes: This is one of France's many 'Tilleuls de Sully', lindens traditionally linked to Maximilien de Bethune, Duke of Sully and minister to Henri IV, who as grand voyer (chief roads officer) promoted planting trees (lime or elm) at village churches and squares around 1599-1600 after the Wars of Religion. NOTE: an earlier pass in this same leads file (see the blocked 'Tilleuls de Sully' entry, verified 2026-09-04) correctly ruled that 'Tilleuls de Sully' as a category is NOT a collectible point because it names dozens of independently planted trees, not one famous tree. This entry is different: it is a single, individually named and documented specimen, 'Le Sully de Pesselieres', which is why it was kept as a separate open lead rather than folded into that block. Age basis: the French Wikipedia article for Pesselieres states plainly, with a direct citation to a named 2013 article in the regional newspaper L'Yonne republicaine ('A Sougeres-en-Puisaye, bien plus qu'un arbre, un symbole'), that 'Le tilleul "Le Sully" de Pesselieres a ete plante en 1598' (planted in 1598), and that in 1998 two days of festival marked its 400th anniversary. This is a documented planting date for THIS specific tree (not a bridge claim inferred from a general Sully legend elsewhere), so I used it directly: 2026 minus 1598 is 428 years, and I gave it a narrow +/-5 year band since the source states the date as settled fact with a named celebration attached to it, rather than treating it as loosely as a vague oral tradition. Continuity evidence: Wikipedia's own gallery includes a photo captioned 'Le Sully de Pesselieres au debut du XXe siecle' (early 20th century) alongside one from 2014, and Commons holds further dated photographs from 23 February 2008 and 26 April 2014, so there is a documented visual record spanning over a century, which is unusually strong continuity evidence for this batch. Alive/visited evidence: Visorando (an active French hiking-route platform) lists 13 different hiking routes passing 'Tilleul de Sully de Pesseliere' with an aggregate rating of 4.3/5 from 14 reviews, which is real, current evidence of people still visiting on foot, stronger than anything found for the other candidates in this batch. Girth: no source I found gives a circumference figure for this specific tree (general 'Tilleul de Sully' surveys elsewhere put the type's average around 5-7m, but that is about OTHER trees of the same planting tradition and would be a bridge claim if applied here, so I left girth_cm empty rather than borrow a number from a different tree). Location precision: I could not independently cross-check the given coordinate against an EXIF/OSM geotag the way I could for two of the other candidates in this batch, so despite the tree being a single well-documented named specimen in a tiny hamlet, I am marking this approximate rather than confirmed to stay honest about that gap. Destination test: of the five candidates in this batch, I would rate this one as clearing the bar most comfortably alongside the Jauze yew: it has a firm, celebrated, single-tree history (a real quadricentennial festival), over a century of photographic documentation, and demonstrable, current hiker interest via a real ratings platform, which together read as more than a passing regional curiosity.
